analysis.title: Beyond the Earnings Boom (Global Equity Observer, International Equity Team, October 2026)
key_insights: Q3 2026 was a challenging quarter for global markets. Re-escalating U.S.-Iran tensions and tighter supply drove Brent crude futures up 40%, keeping inflation fears in focus.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose 50 bps over September to close at 5.29%, its highest level in more than two decades, as central banks raised policy rates and fiscal and sovereign debt concerns weighed on long-duration bonds.

Equities were choppy. July saw a reversal in AI infrastructure beneficiaries, with semiconductors falling sharply. Most losses were recovered by September after releases of next-generation autonomous agents and frontier models improved AI sentiment.

Market participation narrowed over the quarter. Less than one-third of MSCI World constituents outperformed the index in September, down from about two-thirds in July. The team's quality portfolios' relative performance followed the same round trip.

MSCI World gained 2% in Q3 and 12% year-to-date. Its 12-month forward EPS is up 23% year-to-date while its multiple fell 10% to 18x NTM P/E, versus a COVID-era peak of 21x and a 10-year average of 17x. S&P 500 forward EPS is up 31% year-to-date.
Earnings strength is broad: only four of 11 MSCI World sectors (utilities, health care, consumer staples, real estate) have EPS growth below 10%. Most upgrades come from energy and AI.

Energy EPS is up 60% year-to-date. Semiconductors are +111%, hardware +38% and hyperscalers +32%. Energy plus these three AI-enabler groups explain over 70% of the increase in index earnings growth, and concentration is likely higher once AI-driven industrials are counted.

Quality concern 1: earnings growth is not matched by cash generation. MSCI World forward EPS is up 23% year-to-date, but free cash flow growth is 12 percentage points lower. Semiconductor and infrastructure providers take 100% of AI build-out revenue and profit now, while spenders capitalise most of their costs.

Quality concern 2: earnings growth starts from margins already near historical highs. AI productivity gains in advertising and coding have not yet produced a material earnings benefit across the wider corporate sector, so margin gains sit with AI enablers rather than adopters.

Test 1: whether corporates can sustain earnings in a higher-inflation world. High inflation has historically not raised returns on equity, since capital needed to sustain a business rises with prices. Low-quality firms may show temporary pricing power that fades as inflation persists and rates raise input and labour costs.

Test 2: whether the AI earnings boom lasts. It depends on durable pricing power across the supply chain. The usual capital-cycle pattern is that high returns draw new capacity, though short replacement cycles for leading-edge AI chips could keep demand recurring.

Memory operating margins have moved from a historical through-cycle range of about 0%-30% to 70%-80%. Whether this is durable or a traditional capital cycle is described as enormously consequential for the area.
Earnings accretion above 20% in the first nine months of the year has rarely been seen outside recoveries from COVID or the Global Financial Crisis, and never from such a high margin base.

The team favours quality compounders, which it says offer resilient growth and proven pricing power with lower sensitivity to AI build-out, commodity prices and inflation cycles. The premium for dependable earnings growth has compressed.

The team's global portfolios trade at roughly the same free cash flow yield as the market, a valuation rarely seen in their history, despite higher returns on operating capital employed and gross margins. The portfolios are split across AI enablers and bottlenecks, high quality AI adopters at depressed valuations, and defensive compounders.

sector_views.rationale: Energy EPS is up 60% year-to-date on persistently high oil prices. The report calls this earnings contribution volatile and dependent on energy prices.
EPS is up 111% year-to-date. The report questions durability, citing capital-cycle risk and memory margins of 70%-80% against a historical 0%-30%.
Hardware EPS is up 38% and hyperscalers 32%. Hyperscalers capitalise most of their AI costs, so cash generation lags earnings.
Resilient growth, proven pricing power and lower sensitivity to AI, commodities and inflation, at a free cash flow yield in line with the market.

earnings_insights: MSCI World 12-month forward EPS is up 23% year-to-date (forward estimate, as of 30 September 2026). S&P 500 forward EPS is up 31% year-to-date.
Year-to-date forward EPS growth by group: energy +60%, semiconductors +111%, hardware +38%, hyperscalers +32%. Together these explain over 70% of the index's earnings growth increase.
Only utilities, health care, consumer staples and real estate have forward EPS growth below 10% among MSCI World's 11 sectors.
Forward free cash flow growth for MSCI World is 12 percentage points below the 23% forward EPS growth.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Month-end close, up 50 bps over the month and the highest in more than two decades. Long-duration bonds are under pressure from inflation fears, central bank hikes and fiscal concerns.
The energy shock from re-escalating U.S.-Iran tensions and tight supply kept inflation fears in focus and drove energy earnings.
Modest quarterly gain on strong earnings growth, with the multiple compressing.
Down 10% year-to-date, below the 21x COVID-era peak and slightly above the 17x 10-year average.

risk_factors: Earnings growth is concentrated in energy and AI-enabler groups (over 70% of the increase), so it depends on volatile oil prices and AI capital spending.
Free cash flow growth trails EPS growth by 12 percentage points, so underlying corporate economics improve less than headline earnings.
Corporate margins start near historical highs, and AI productivity gains have not yet reached adopters' earnings.
Higher inflation and rising rates raise capital needs and input and labour costs, which can erode returns on equity.
AI capital cycle: high returns could draw new supply and compress economics, particularly in memory.
Central bank rate hikes, fiscal pressure and sovereign debt concerns weigh on long-duration bonds.
vol_and_positioning: Participation narrowed: under one-third of MSCI World constituents outperformed the index in September, versus about two-thirds in July.
July saw a sharp reversal in semiconductors and other physical AI infrastructure names, largely recovered by September.
geopolitical: Re-escalating U.S.-Iran tensions and tightening supply drove Brent crude futures up 40% in Q3 2026.

tension_points.bull_case: Supply constraints may persist and the short replacement cycle for leading-edge AI chips could create recurring demand that sustains today's economics.
tension_points.bear_case: Under the usual capital-cycle pattern, exceptional returns draw new capacity and margins fall. Memory operating margins of 70%-80% against a historical 0%-30% make this especially consequential.

tension_points.bull_case: Forward EPS is up 23% year-to-date on a broad base, with only four of 11 sectors below 10% growth.
tension_points.bear_case: Free cash flow growth is 12 percentage points lower than EPS growth, and margins start near historical highs.

theme_stances.evidence: the earnings boom has not been matched by cash generation

theme_stances.key_argument: Quality compounders offer resilient growth and pricing power with low sensitivity to AI, commodities and inflation, at valuations in line with the market.
theme_stances.evidence: we find the opportunity in quality compounders particularly compelling
